prompt.context: Your client is the State Department of Education and it is looking to improve the education outcomes of the general population. The department believes that investment in Pre-Kindergarten education (ages 3-4) is key and wants to increase the capacity of its state-accredited Pre-K programs. The client is thinking about running a campaign to raise taxes to fund this initiative.
prompt.question: The client has come to us with three questions: 1. How many additional spots for children need to be funded for the Pre-K programs? 2. How much will the campaign cost? 3. How should they approach the tax increase campaign?

clarifying_info.q: What does 'improving education outcomes' mean exactly?
clarifying_info.a: Education outcome means college admittance and completion rates.

clarifying_info.q: Are there private Pre-K programs we can partner with?
clarifying_info.a: Private Pre-K programs are highly fragmented and range widely in quality. The State Department of Education only wants to rely on state-funded programs where they can guarantee quality (education level of teacher, full-day program with adequate teaching materials/supplies, etc.).

clarifying_info.q: Is the program free or does it generate revenue?
clarifying_info.a: No revenues — the program will be free. The state wants to limit capacity to only children from low-income families who could not afford private programs.

clarifying_info.q: What does it cost to add a spot?
clarifying_info.a: Cost per spot is $10,000 per year to the state.

clarifying_info.q: Has the state run a similar program before?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The State Department of Education has already launched a similar initiative and provided some funding. Now they want to expand the program.

clarifying_info.q: How is the state population distributed by age?
clarifying_info.a: Population is experiencing steady growth. Assume equal distribution of children in each age among all kids ages 3 through 18 (K-12th grade equivalent).

clarifying_info.q: What were the results of the existing program?
clarifying_info.a: The graduates of last year's program did not show great results when tested on social and aptitude-for-learning skills (how long they can sit still, how they interact with other kids). The State Department of Education hopes the poor results may be due to flaws in the test.

exhibits.title: Regional Pre-K Supply and Demand Data
exhibits.shows: A table with five regions listing Population (K-12th grade), % Low Income, and Current Spots Available. The candidate must calculate how many Pre-K spots are needed in each region and compare to current supply.

exhibits.title: Regional Border Proximity Map
exhibits.shows: A map or chart showing what percentage of each region's residents live within 30 minutes of a neighboring region's border, highlighting potential for cross-region program access.

data.note: 10-20% of residents in several regions (notably Region 3 and Region 5) live less than 30 minutes from the border of an adjacent region

framework: Financial considerations: Total addressable market (Pre-K children of low-income families) vs. current capacity by region; cost to add new spots ($10K/spot/year); taxpayer base and mechanism for tax increase
Strategic considerations: Benchmarks from other states that have launched Pre-K programs; role (if any) of private Pre-K providers; competing priorities for state/district resources

Operational considerations: Long-term impact of funding initiative to build taxpayer support; what is being taxed (real estate, sales, etc.) and who bears the burden; reallocation of existing over-funded spots before new spending

questions.prompt: Question 1: How many additional spots need to be funded to reach the goal of providing Pre-K education to all low-income children? (Use Exhibit 1)
questions.guidance: Strong answer walks through each region step by step: (1) derive Pre-K population from K-12 population assuming equal age distribution across 16 age cohorts (ages 3-18), so Pre-K (ages 3-4) = 2/16 of K-12 pop; (2) multiply by % low-income to get spots needed; (3) compare to current spots to find surplus/deficit. Candidate should note that Regions 2, 4, and 5 are OVERFUNDED and flag that reallocation should happen before any new tax campaign. Total net additional spots needed is fewer than 400.

math.setup: Pre-K pop = K-12 pop × (2/16). Spots needed = Pre-K pop × % low-income. Net = Spots needed − Current spots available.
steps: Total net: 38 + 353 − 2,229 − 2,079 − 825 = −4,742 (system-wide surplus of ~4,742 spots; only 391 net new spots are needed in Regions 1 and 3, but system overall has massive over-capacity)
math.answer: Regions 1 and 3 need 38 and 353 additional spots respectively (391 total). Regions 2, 4, and 5 are overfunded by a combined ~5,133 spots. Net system-wide new spots needed: fewer than 400. Reallocation should be explored before raising taxes.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Given the overfunding in some regions, what does Exhibit 2 tell you, and what are the implications for the campaign?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that Exhibit 2 shows geographic proximity: 10-20% of residents in regions near the border could feasibly attend schools in an adjacent region. This suggests: (a) students from underfunded Regions 1 and 3 who live near the borders of Regions 2 and 4 could attend schools with surplus capacity; (b) teachers from overfunded regions could be redeployed to underfunded regions. Candidate should also flag practical barriers for low-income families: lack of transportation, inability to drive children to another region. Strong candidate questions whether the 10-20% border population overlaps with the low-income target demographic and whether adjacent regions are in fact Regions 2 or 4.

questions.prompt: Question 3 / Elevator pitch: Should the client launch a tax campaign to fund expansion? What is your recommendation?
questions.guidance: Strong answer synthesizes: (1) no new net spots needed at system level — reallocation comes first; (2) existing program results are inconclusive/poor, so expanding before improving quality is premature; (3) therefore, do NOT recommend launching a tax campaign at this time. Should recommend fixing program quality and reallocating resources first, then reassess.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the benefits of improving Pre-K education outcomes?

categories.name: Short-term education goals
ideas: Building attention span (ability to sit still)

categories.name: Long-term education goals
ideas: Reading and writing at grade level
Higher college admittance and completion rates

categories.name: Broader societal / economic benefits
ideas: Higher workforce participation and tax base
Attracting and retaining residents in the state

recommendation: Do NOT recommend launching a tax increase campaign or expanding the program at this time

First reallocate the approximately 5,000 surplus spots from Regions 2, 4, and 5 to serve the deficits in Regions 1 and 3 — this can be done by redeploying teachers or, where geographically feasible, routing border-adjacent low-income children to schools in neighboring regions
The existing program's poor results suggest a quality or measurement problem that must be resolved before scaling
risks: The state continues to fall behind education standards, making it harder to attract and retain residents — inaction has long-term costs
Poor test results may reflect a flawed assessment instrument rather than a truly ineffective program — if the test is flawed, the program may be better than it appears
Reallocation across regions faces practical barriers for low-income families (transportation, time)
next_steps: Audit current program curriculum and teaching quality to diagnose why outcomes are poor
Validate or redesign the social/aptitude assessment used to measure program effectiveness
Model reallocation options: teacher transfers vs. cross-region student placement, factoring in transportation access
Revisit expansion and tax campaign only after demonstrating replicable positive results from the existing program
